blocks.text: A mini-batch is a small subset of the full training dataset, processed together in one training step, striking a practical middle ground between updating weights after every single example and waiting to process the entire dataset before making any update at all.

Understanding mini-batches sets up several other topics in this module, gradient accumulation, learning rate, and scheduling all build on the basic idea of training happening one mini-batch at a time.
1. What a Mini-Batch Actually Is

blocks.alt: The full dataset gets split into mini-batches, and one mini-batch is processed at a time

blocks.text: Rather than processing the entire training dataset in one pass, or one example at a time, training splits the dataset into small groups, mini-batches, and processes one mini-batch per training step, computing gradients and updating weights based on that group of examples together.
2. Why Not Train on One Example at a Time

blocks.alt: Training one example at a time produces noisy, slow progress

blocks.text: Updating weights after every single example produces a very noisy training signal, each individual example gradient can point in a somewhat different direction, and training also fails to take advantage of modern hardware, which is specifically optimized to process many examples in parallel rather than one at a time.
3. Why Not Train on the Whole Dataset at Once

blocks.alt: Processing the whole dataset at once needs too much memory

blocks.text: At the other extreme, computing a gradient using the entire dataset at once would produce a very smooth, stable gradient signal, but would require holding an enormous amount of data and intermediate computation in memory simultaneously, quickly becoming impractical for any dataset of meaningful size.
4. Mini-Batches and Parallel Hardware

blocks.alt: A mini-batch enables parallel GPU compute

blocks.text: A mini-batch sized to take advantage of GPU parallelism lets many examples be processed simultaneously as one batched operation, dramatically faster than processing examples one by one, which is why mini-batch sizes are often chosen partly based on what a given GPU can efficiently process in parallel.

code.content:
# A simplified mini-batch training loop
for mini_batch in dataloader:
    predictions = model(mini_batch.inputs)
    loss = compute_loss(predictions, mini_batch.targets)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
    optimizer.zero_grad()

blocks.text: 5. Mini-Batch Size vs Gradient Noise

blocks.alt: A small batch produces noisier gradients while a large batch produces smoother gradients

blocks.text: A smaller mini-batch produces a noisier, less stable gradient estimate for each training step, while a larger mini-batch produces a smoother, more stable estimate, closer to what the full dataset gradient would look like, though at the cost of using more memory per step.

blocks.text: 6. Choosing a Mini-Batch Size in Practice

The practical mini-batch size a team can use is often set by available GPU memory as much as by any theoretical ideal, and the gradient accumulation technique covered in the next topic of this module exists specifically to work around this constraint when a larger effective batch size would be preferable but memory does not allow it directly.
7. Mini-Batches Across an Epoch

blocks.alt: Batch one, batch two, and batch three lead to the end of an epoch

blocks.text: One full epoch, a complete pass through the training dataset covered in earlier fine-tuning workflow discussions, consists of processing every mini-batch in the dataset exactly once, in whatever order the dataset shuffling, covered in the Dataset Preparation module, determined.
8. Mini-Batches and Memory

blocks.alt: A larger batch size requires more memory per training step

blocks.title: This connects directly to the earlier Training Large Models on Limited GPUs topic
blocks.content: Mini-batch size is one of the most direct levers for controlling training memory usage, alongside quantization and gradient checkpointing covered in the LoRA and QLoRA module.

blocks.text: Because activations for every example in a mini-batch need to be stored during the forward pass for use during backpropagation, memory usage scales directly with mini-batch size, making it one of the first settings to adjust when a training run does not fit in available memory.
9. Mini-Batches Relative to Gradient Accumulation

Gradient accumulation, covered in full in the next topic, lets a team use a small mini-batch size for memory reasons while still achieving the training dynamics of a much larger effective batch, a technique that only makes sense once the basic mini-batch idea covered here is well understood.
Worked Example

A team fine-tuning on a dataset of ten thousand examples uses a mini-batch size of 16, meaning each training step processes 16 examples together, computing one combined gradient and update from them, and a full epoch requires roughly six hundred twenty five such steps to work through the entire dataset once.

When they try increasing the mini-batch size to 64 for smoother gradients, they run into a memory error on their available GPU, leading them to explore gradient accumulation, covered next, as a way to get the benefits of a larger effective batch without the memory cost of processing it all at once.
Common Mistakes

items: Choosing a mini-batch size so small that gradient noise makes training unstable
Choosing a mini-batch size so large it exceeds available memory without considering gradient accumulation as an alternative
Confusing mini-batch size with the total dataset size or the number of epochs
Not accounting for how mini-batch size interacts with learning rate, a connection covered further in the Learning Rate topic

blocks.text: Practice

For a dataset size and mini-batch size of your choosing, calculate how many training steps make up one full epoch, confirming you understand the direct relationship between dataset size, batch size, and steps per epoch.
Key Takeaway

A mini-batch is a small group of training examples processed together in one training step, striking a practical balance between the instability of updating on single examples and the memory cost of processing an entire dataset at once, with its size directly shaping both gradient stability and memory usage during training.
